title: Peltola Flips Alaska Senate Seat, Giving Democrats a 56–44 Majority
excerpt: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, the Associated Press called the race Tuesday, Nov. 17 — the last Senate contest
content:
Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, the Associated Press called the race Tuesday, Nov. 17 — the last Senate contest of the 2026 midterms to be decided, two weeks after Election Day.

With about 99% of votes counted, Peltola had 144,302 votes (50.12%) to Sullivan's 131,844 (45.80%), according to the AP. Clearing 50% matters because Alaska uses ranked-choice voting — a first-choice majority wins outright, with no further rounds needed.

The win gives Democrats a 56–44 majority in the U.S. Senate, their largest since 2009. Republicans entered the midterms with a 53–47 majority. The new balance takes effect in January 2027, not immediately.

It was the ninth Republican-held Senate seat Democrats flipped in this midterm cycle, the most flips in a midterm since 1958, according to the AP.

Peltola, 53, is the first Alaska Native ever elected to the U.S. Senate, according to Reuters. She was previously the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress, holding Alaska's lone U.S. House seat, and she is only the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the Senate. Before entering politics, she worked in the commercial fishing industry.

In the open primary, Peltola finished first with 49.5% to Sullivan's 41.4%, according to the AP. A same-name candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, finished a distant third but advanced as a top-four finisher. The AP reported that the race was roiled before the election by allegations that members of Peltola's campaign helped recruit the same-name candidate; that allegation rests in part on a Times report based on texts, documents and interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, who was fired shortly before the primary and later sought to recant. Webb Watch is reporting that as an allegation, not as established fact.

As part of the same Nov. 3 election, Alaskans also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins — a result Webb Watch reported Nov. 15.

What it means for readers here: with Democrats now holding the Senate 56–44 — and the House as well, according to Reuters — the incoming Congress that Rep. Henry Cuellar (TX-28, Laredo) will work with is Democratic-controlled in both chambers. That matters for border, trade and port-of-entry funding that directly affects Laredo. The AP also noted Democrats won campaigns in other conservative states this cycle, including the Senate race in Texas.

The result is a media projection, not yet a certified result. Webb Watch will update this story when Alaska certifies the vote.
